title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "The findings of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages in communication by Albert Mehrabian and his colleagues at UCLA in 1967 have been quoted so frequently that they are now often regarded as a self-evident truth."
Why: The passage discusses a study comparing verbal and non-verbal messages, which corresponds to the "effects" (or impact) of these communication types being evaluated in the experiments.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In the first experiment, subjects were asked to listen to a recording of a female saying the word "maybe" in three tones of voice to convey liking, neutrality and disliking."
Why: The subjects in both experiments were asked to guess the emotions or attitudes of the speaker, which is paraphrased in the summary as identifying the "feelings" being communicated.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "The subjects were then shown photos of female faces expressing the same three emotions and were asked to guess the emotions in the recorded voice and the photos."
Why: The first experiment compared voice tones with photos of faces, which corresponds to "facial expressions" in the word bank.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Three words had positive meanings (e.g. honey), three were neutral (e.g. oh) and three were negative (e.g. terrible)."
Why: The second experiment focused on tone of voice alongside the individual words used, matching the option "word meanings".

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "The first is that the entire study involved only 62 subjects."
Why: The statement claims that having too few subjects was a limitation, which directly matches the writer's view that the small sample size (only 62 subjects) was a methodological limitation.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "Thus, the findings may simply be a product of the nature of the sample."
Why: The statement claims that the subjects' similar backgrounds were an advantage, whereas the writer views this uniformity as a negative limitation that makes the findings unreliable.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "Critics have also pointed out that the 7-38-55 formula is flawed since it was pieced together from two different experiments, neither of which involved all three channels (verbal, vocal, and facial)."
Why: The passage discusses flaws in how the experiments were combined, but the writer never expresses an opinion on whether the two experiments should have been carried out in a different order.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 11
Quote: "The researchers intentionally used a "neutral" word so naturally the subjects found little meaning there."
Why: The statement claims the choice of a neutral word was helpful, but the writer views it negatively, stating that it naturally resulted in subjects finding little meaning and lacked validity.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In the first experiment, subjects were asked to listen to a recording of a female saying the word "maybe" in three tones of voice to convey liking, neutrality and disliking."
Why: The passage mentions the use of a single word ("maybe") in English, but the writer never discusses whether including a range of languages would have made the study more valid.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 15
Quote: "Clearly, one appealing aspect of the Mehrabian study is its numerical precision."
Why: Option C restates this as "It makes the claims more attractive" by matching "appealing aspect" to "more attractive".

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 17
Quote: "There is a certain mystique about non-verbal communication, and the continued references to this research sustain it, encouraging people to believe in the overwhelming importance of the non-verbal message compared with the verbal one."
Why: Option A restates this by explaining that prioritizing non-verbal messages leads to an undervaluing of language.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 18
Quote: "If we could communicate 93% of information and attitudes with vocal and facial cues, it would be wasteful to spend time learning a language"
Why: Option B restates this by pointing out that because we do spend time learning language, it must be important.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 20
Quote: "Please remember that all my findings… dealt with communications of feelings and attitudes…"
Why: Option D restates this by indicating that the findings apply to only one specific area (feelings and attitudes) rather than all communication.

title: A closer examination of a study on verbal and non-verbal messages
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 21
Quote: "To be fair, many textbook writers attempt to be faithful to the context of Mehrabian’s research."
Why: Option C restates this as presenting varying interpretations, because the paragraph goes on to show how different authors interpret and explain the research in various ways.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Schlaug’s research suggests that with intensive therapy, some patients can even move from this two-tone singing back to actual speech."
Why: Option D correctly states that stroke patients may regain speech if they receive music therapy daily, which is paraphrased here as intensive therapy.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "When she opens her hand, I see that this ‘leaf’— perhaps 40 millimetres long—has tiny, almost bird-like feet, a pair of onyx-black eyes and appears to have been sprinkled with glitter."
Why: The text states that the frog is "perhaps 40 millimetres long", which matches the summary's requirement for its length.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "The glossy lime-green frogs that can be heard croaking to one another from farm ponds and rivers are in fact Australian imports; New Zealand native frogs are a very different creature."
Why: The passage describes other frogs making a "croaking" sound, which links to the summary's reference to the noise made by most other frogs.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "They are silent, and consequently, in the evolutionary process, they have lost their eardrums as well, therefore making it easier for researchers like Lukis to trap them."
Why: Because the frogs are silent, they have lost their "eardrums" over time, directly answering why they no longer possess them.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Another behaviour that is unusual for frogs is that the Maud Island species avoid water, so their tiny feet have no webs between their toes, which would normally make swimming and movement in the water more effective."
Why: Since they avoid water, their feet have no "webs" between the toes, fitting the gap about what forest-dwelling frogs do not need.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "Since a tadpole cannot move or survive on dry land, this stage is absent in Maud Island frogs and they go straight from gelatinous eggs (incubated by the males) to ‘froglets’, which spend their first few weeks of life as passengers on the back of a male."
Why: The text explicitly mentions that the "tadpole" stage is absent, meaning they skip this usual phase of development.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "Before the first humans arrived, the frogs’ enemies were predators that hunted by sight—native birds such as weka, morepork and perhaps pukeko—so they developed a simple but effective defence: they kept very still."
Why: FLAG: The direct answer regarding who carries the froglets is found in the sentence "eggs (incubated by the males) to ‘froglets’, which spend their first few weeks of life as passengers on the back of a male" in Paragraph C.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "Her shot reveals patterns and colouration unique to each frog, so that she can identify them without resorting to invasive alternatives like toe-clipping."
Why: This sentence explains the photographic method researchers use to tell individual frogs apart instead of using invasive techniques like toe-clipping.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "In 1997, however, the Department of Conservation moved 300 to Motuara Island, then another 100 to Long Island in 2005."
Why: This sentence details the chronological steps and locations involved in relocating the Maud Island frogs for conservation.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "However, New Zealand came to the surface just in time to provide a lifeboat for the prehistoric frogs to avoid the fate of the relatives they left behind."
Why: This explains that the ancient frogs survived extinction because New Zealand emerged from the sea to act as a "lifeboat" for them.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "The glossy lime-green frogs that can be heard croaking to one another from farm ponds and rivers are in fact Australian imports; New Zealand native frogs are a very different creature."
Why: This compares the introduced Australian frogs with the native New Zealand species, highlighting their differences in appearance and sound.

title: A great leap forward
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "If Lukis can prove that the frogs can cope with mice, it would make more islands available to wildlife managers looking for extra homes for them."
Why: This outlines the broader conservation benefits and range of possibilities that studying the impact of mice on frogs will uncover.

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "'The truth is that such a four-day week has many attractions but it will not be appropriate in every instance,' says Professor Hazel."
Why: Professor Hazel points out that the four-day week initiative "will not be appropriate in every instance," matching the idea that it may not be suitable for all businesses.

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "Anthropologists calculate that in the Stone Age, approximately one to two million years ago, the ancestors of modern humans worked on average two or three hours a day hunting and gathering food."
Why: This sentence gives an exact calculation by anthropologists of the time spent working by ancient humans ("two or three hours a day").

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Roland Gillespie, workplace relations minister in the New Zealand government, described the findings as ‘enormously encouraging’ and said that he was keen to see businesses experiment with similar new and improved work models."
Why: Roland Gillespie, a government minister, expressed his desire to see businesses try new work models, which matches the description of a politician interested in changing how working lives are organized.

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Ryan Schmidt, the director of human resources at MEdia, says that ‘productivity in the economy generally has increased significantly over the last 50 years but there’s a common perception in the workforce that standards of living have not kept pace."
Why: The phrase "productivity... has increased significantly" corresponds to working harder, and "standards of living have not kept pace" matches the feeling that lives have not improved.

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "'This term work–life balance has become a cliché,' says Hadi."
Why: The statement says that a commonly used expression ("work-life balance") is unhelpful because it oversimplifies things; Hadi calls it a "cliché" that has "limited value" because life is an "intricate mix" that cannot be neatly divided.

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "The chief executive of Certified Life, Tane Robinson, says that the four-day week boosted the firm’s reputation and made it easier to retain staff who might otherwise have moved on."
Why: Robinson notes that the company's reputation was boosted (people had a higher opinion of the business) and that it was easier to retain staff (workers were happy to continue working for it).

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Says Deng, ‘Our research found that when employees have greater individual choice and responsibility for their work time, they still devote some of those “free” hours to fulfilling their normal working roles."
Why: Carla Deng states that when employees are given more personal time ("free" hours with greater choice), they still use some of that time to do their normal work, which benefits the company.

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "However, psychologist Dr Gina McDowell argues that the problem of stress caused by working too many hours still doesn’t receive sufficient recognition and ought to be addressed with greater commitment by executives, employees and academics."
Why: Dr McDowell points out that over-working (working too many hours) does not receive enough recognition (is not realised enough) and needs to be taken more seriously (addressed with greater commitment) by those involved.

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Lead researcher Dr Hannah Graham says that the experiment produced such positive results partly because employees were given a role in decision-making throughout it."
Why: Dr Graham explains that the trial succeeded because staff were involved at every stage of organising it ("given a role in decision-making throughout it").

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "The experiment was conducted at Certified Life, a firm which has sold insurance for more than six decades."
Why: The question asks what service the company (Certified Life) provided, and the text explicitly states that it has sold "insurance".

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "The 240 employees at Certified Life completed surveys at the beginning and end of the experiment to provide information for the study."
Why: The question asks about the research method used to gather data, and the text shows that employees filled out "surveys" at the start and end of the experiment.

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Furthermore, cooperation between employees was seen to improve significantly when working shorter hours and team cohesion was significantly enhanced, according to the supervisors."
Why: The question asks which group of people reported that staff worked together more closely (cooperation improved), and the text identifies this group as the "supervisors".

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Quite apart from the benefits at Certified Life, Dr Graham also suggests that such schemes might address the issue of congestion in major cities by restricting the numbers going to work each day."
Why: The question asks what problem outside the workplace might be addressed by shorter hours, and Dr Graham suggests it could solve the issue of "congestion".

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "‘The truth is that such a four-day week has many attractions but it will not be appropriate in every instance,’ says Professor Hazel."
Why: Professor Hazel's statement that the four-day week "will not be appropriate in every instance" directly matches the prompt's claim that a workplace initiative may not be suitable for all businesses.

title: Achieving a Work–Life Balance
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "This term work–life balance has become a cliché,"
Why: The passage describes "work–life balance" as a "cliché" that has "limited value," which restates the idea that a commonly used expression is unhelpful because it oversimplifies reality.

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "Though we might think of film as an essentially visual experience, we really cannot afford to underestimate the importance of film sound."
Why: Option B restates "cannot afford to underestimate the importance of film sound" as "it would be wrong to overlook the contribution of sound".

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Often with film characterization the audience perceives little or no difference between the character and the actor."
Why: Option C restates the idea that audiences see "little or no difference" between the actor and the character as "the importance of the actor and the character appearing to have similar personalities".

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "For example, in the highly successful science-fiction film 2001, little dialogue was evident, and most of it was banal and of little intrinsic interest."
Why: Option B restates the use of "banal" (dull) dialogue in 2001 to portray the inadequacy of human responses as meaning that dull dialogue can have a specific purpose.

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "This use of dialogue underscores not only the dizzy quality of the character played by Katherine Hepburn, but also the absurdity of the film itself and thus its humor."
Why: Option B restates how the rapid dialogue "underscores" the character's dizzy quality and the film's absurdity as "the nature of the dialogue emphasises key elements of the film."

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "However, if the 'click' of an opening door is part of an ominous action such as a burglary, the sound mixer may call attention to the 'click' with an increase in volume; this helps to engage the audience in a moment of suspense."
Why: Option C restates how increasing the volume of a realistic sound to create suspense means that realistic sounds "may be modified in order to manipulate the audience's response".

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "We are probably all familiar with background music in films, which has become so ubiquitous as to be noticeable in its absence."
Why: "Ubiquitous" means it is everywhere, and being "noticeable in its absence" directly matches the idea that audiences would find it surprising if it were missing.

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "In addition, background music often foreshadows a change in mood."
Why: "Foreshadows" means it shows or indicates something beforehand, which matches the idea that music may anticipate a development.

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Usually not meant to be noticeable, it often provides a tone or an emotional attitude toward the story and/or the characters depicted."
Why: The passage discusses what background music generally does for audiences as a whole, but it is completely silent on whether it has a stronger effect on some individuals than on others (a comparison).

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Background music may aid viewer understanding by linking scenes."
Why: "Linking scenes" matches the idea that the music helps the audience to make connections between different parts of the film.

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "The effects of sound are often largely subtle and often are noted by only our subconscious minds."
Why: The passage states that the effects are usually noted only by our subconscious minds, which contradicts the statement that audiences tend to be aware of how the music is affecting them.

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "These three tracks must be mixed and balanced so as to produce the necessary emphases which in turn create desired effects."
Why: Mixing and balancing the three tracks (voice, sound, and music) appropriately allows the film-maker to control the necessary emphases and create the desired responses or effects in the audience.

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "As is the case with stage drama, dialogue serves to tell the story and expresses feelings and motivations of characters as well."
Why: Listening to the dialogue allows the audience to understand the story as well as the feelings and motivations of the characters.

title: An Introduction to Film Sound
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "When voice textures fit the performer's physiognomy and gestures, a whole and very realistic persona emerges."
Why: A character feels like a real person instead of an actor when the performer's appearance (physiognomy), voice textures, and movements (gestures) all match and are consistent.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Most people can readily conjure images inside their head – known as their mind’s eye. But this year scientists have described a condition, aphantasia, in which some people are unable to visualise mental images."
Why: The passage says people with aphantasia are completely *unable* to visualise mental images, whereas the statement claims it is merely *hard* for them to do so.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "I couldn’t see any sheep jumping over fences, there was nothing to count."
Why: Niel confirms he could not picture the sheep in his head, which directly matches the statement that he was unable to count sheep in his mind.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "When I think about my fiancée there is no image, but I am definitely thinking about her, I know today she has her hair up at the back, she’s brunette."
Why: The passage mentions that Niel remembers his fiancée's features and hair, but the text is completely silent on whether people with aphantasia generally struggle to remember the personal traits and clothes of *different* people.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "The response from his mates is a very sympathetic: “You’re weird.” But while Niel is very relaxed about his inability to picture things, it is often a cause of distress for others."
Why: The statement accurately reflects the passage's claim that the inability to picture things is often a cause of distress for others.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "One person who took part in a study into aphantasia said he had started to feel “isolated” and “alone” after discovering that other people could see images in their heads."
Why: While one participant in a study felt isolated and alone, the passage does not state that *all* people with aphantasia experience these feelings at some point in their lives.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Her career relies on the vivid images that leap into her mind’s eye when she reads text from her author."
Why: The passage states that Lauren's career relies on her vivid mental images, which means the same thing as depending on her imagination.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "When I met her in her box-room studio in Manchester, she was working on a dramatic scene in the next book."
Why: The passage states that Lauren was working on a *dramatic* scene when the author met her, whereas the statement claims she was working on a *comedy* scene.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "Not many people have mental imagery as vibrant as Lauren or as blank as Niel."
Why: The text states that "Not many people" have imagination as "vibrant" as Lauren's.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "Adam Zeman, a professor of cognitive and behavioural neurology, wants to compare the lives and experiences of people with aphantasia and its polar-opposite hyperphantasia."
Why: Hyperphantasia is described as the "polar-opposite" of aphantasia.

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 11
Quote: "How we imagine is clearly very subjective – one person’s vivid scene could be another’s grainy picture."
Why: The passage contrasts one person's vivid scene with another person's "grainy picture".

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 12
Quote: "He is adamant that aphantasia is “not a disorder” and says it may affect up to one in 50 people."
Why: Prof Zeman is "adamant" that the condition is not a disorder (or illness).

title: Aphantasia: A life without mental images
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 12
Quote: "I think it makes quite an important difference to their experience of life because many of us spend our lives with imagery hovering somewhere in the mind’s eye which we inspect from time to time, it’s a variability of human experience."
Why: Many people spend their lives with "imagery hovering" in their mind's eye.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "(1) Only natural processes, such as volcanic eruptions and variations in solar output, caused periods of relative warming and cooling."
Why: The text states that prior to human industrialisation and the 19th century, only natural processes affected the climate.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "This disparity in warming between the poles and the tropics is a phenomenon known as polar amplification."
Why: The term refers directly to the difference between polar warming and tropical warming mentioned in the notes.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Fresh snow is the brightest natural surface on Earth, as it reflects nearly 85% of solar radiation that hits it."
Why: The text explains that fresh snow reflects the vast majority of sunlight that falls upon it.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "In the springtime, this ice melts and exposes the dark ocean underneath, which leads to warming of the region, and this warming melts even more ice, resulting in a positive feedback loop."
Why: The notes state that ice melts in the springtime, matching the timeframe specified in the text.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "The level of melting of the Greenland ice sheet is a major indicator of potential sea level rise; if it completely melts, global sea levels could rise by as much as 6 metres, endangering coastal cities and small island nations while making dangerous weather events, such as floods and hurricanes, even more deadly."
Why: The passage warns that small island nations and coastal cities are at risk if the Greenland ice sheet disappears.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "The most troubling effect of this feedback loop is the release of methane into the atmosphere."
Why: The notes highlight the risk of methane leakage into the atmosphere as the permafrost thaws.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In fact, the average temperature of Antarctica has not changed in the last several decades, despite an increase in the concentration of greenhouse gases."
Why: The statement claims that temperatures in the Antarctic have increased, but the passage directly contradicts this by stating that the average temperature there has not changed.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "In autumn, large storms in the open ocean create more waves that cause the Arctic waters to mix with warmer waters, which increases the heat absorbed in the summer, making ice formation more difficult again in the autumn."
Why: The passage mentions that wave action affects ice formation in the *autumn*, but it contains no information about waves accelerating the melting of sea ice in the *summer*.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "The level of melting of the Greenland ice sheet is a major indicator of potential sea level rise; if it completely melts, global sea levels could rise by as much as 6 metres, endangering coastal cities and small island nations while making dangerous weather events, such as floods and hurricanes, even more deadly."
Why: The passage confirms that a complete melt of the Greenland ice sheet could cause severe sea level rises that endanger coastal cities and small island nations, matching the statement's claim.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "As this permafrost melts, plants and animals that were frozen under the ice begin to decay, and if there is no restriction on oxygen, this releases mostly carbon dioxide. However, if the soil is waterlogged, fermentation occurs and this discharges a gas called methane."
Why: The passage explains that the presence of water in the soil (making it waterlogged) determines whether fermentation occurs and releases methane rather than carbon dioxide.

title: Arctic Warming
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "This is what plants do naturally, but Direct Air Capture does it much more rapidly and requires less land space."
Why: The passage states that Direct Air Capture removes carbon dioxide "more rapidly" than plants do naturally, which agrees with the statement that it captures carbon dioxide more efficiently.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "The rates of technological progress are far exceeding rates of psychological evolution, leaving us ill-equipped to cope with our lifestyle, which in turn leads to increased stress."
Why: This sentence explains how fast technological change ("rapid change") outpaces our psychological evolution, causing negative effects like being ill-equipped to cope and suffering from increased stress.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Though not technically a biophilic design, Fallingwater – the stunning house in rural Pennsylvania designed in the 1930s by Frank Lloyd Wright - arguably speaks to the human soul much more than the box-like blocks of flats designed by his contemporary Le Corbusier."
Why: Le Corbusier's "box-like blocks of flats" are contrasted with biophilic design, serving as an example of an architect whose creations are uncharacteristic of biophilia.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "The premise of biophilic design seeks both to avoid or minimize harmful impacts on the natural environment, and equally importantly, to provide and restore beneficial contacts between people and nature in the built environment."
Why: This sentence directly defines the two main goals of biophilic design: minimizing harm to the environment and restoring the connection between humans and nature.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph H
Quote: "They mimicked nature's forms, producing magnificent structures with which we are still awed - though biophilic design is a novel concept, they certainly employed some of its recommendations."
Why: This statement praises ancient architects for mimicking nature and creating magnificent structures, matching the positive claim about early forms of architecture.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "All too often, architects have put creative originality before the needs of the people who have to live and work in their futuristic constructions, with scant regard for emotional, as well as practical, considerations."
Why: Putting "creative originality" before human needs matches the idea that architects are too focused on innovation ("creative originality").

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "It harnesses solar power, utilizes both active and passive air systems, and monitors the weather to adapt to conditions."
Why: Harnessing solar power and using active/passive air systems are specific features that conserve energy in the sustainable Lewis Center.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "The rates of technological progress are far exceeding rates of psychological evolution, leaving us ill-equipped to cope with our lifestyle, which in turn leads to increased stress."
Why: The sentence states that progress in technology ("technological advancements") happens at a speed ("so quickly") that humans cannot adjust to.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "The rates of technological progress are far exceeding rates of psychological evolution, leaving us ill-equipped to cope with our lifestyle, which in turn leads to increased stress."
Why: The text explicitly states that our inability to cope with modern lifestyles results in "increased stress," matching the gap's requirement for what biophilia helps us deal with.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "For example, one crucial element of the natural landscape to human health is sunlight."
Why: The passage highlights "sunlight" as a key natural element that people are evolutionarily programmed to respond to positively for their health and well-being.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "One group had a view of a tree; the others had a window looking onto a brick wall."
Why: The experiment compared patients who could see a "tree" with those who looked at a brick wall, noting that the former group experienced faster recoveries.

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "The wall purifies the air and has the potential to fulfill the building's fresh air intake requirements."

title: Biophilic Design

title: Biophilic Design
explanation:

Why: This matches option D because wanting to "redefine the relationship between humankind and the environment" and "expand our sense of ecological possibilities" means it aims to inspire new ways of thinking about the environment.

title: Bird Migration

Why: This sentence directly states the primary motivation behind bird migration, which is the core theme summarized by the heading.

title: Bird Migration

Why: The paragraph details how birds bypass closer, seemingly suitable habitats to travel much further away, matching the idea of rejecting closer feeding grounds.

title: Bird Migration

title: Bird Migration
explanation:

Why: This sentence introduces the paragraph's discussion of scientific discoveries regarding the navigational mechanisms and sensory perceptions birds use during migration.

title: Bird Migration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F

Why: The paragraph explains how birds use barometric pressure and weather forecasting to choose the optimal time to begin their journey.

title: Bird Migration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G

Why: This paragraph illustrates how birds successfully handle and survive strong winds that displace them across oceans, aligning with the heading about managing wind problems.

title: Bird Migration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C

Why: This directly matches the statement that birds often fly further than they need to.

title: Bird Migration
explanation:

title: Bird Migration
explanation:

Why: The question asks how young birds find their wintering grounds without the help of their parents, matching the phrase "without parental guidance" in the text, giving the answer "parental".

title: Bird Migration

title: Bird Migration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Daytime predators are avoided and the danger of dehydration due to flying for long periods in warm, sunlit skies is reduced."
Why: The text explicitly mentions that flying at night helps birds avoid daytime "predators", which corresponds to avoiding contact with them in the summary.

title: Bird Migration
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F

Why: The passage explains that birds react to weather changes before any "visible" signs appear, fitting the idea that they detect weather changes without visible signs.

title: Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "First and foremost, this book is a series of biographical sketches of the key business management thinkers, from Frederick Taylor (the 19th-century industrialist who created scientific management theory) to Peter Drucker (the academic credited with founding modern management in the 1950s)."
Why: The reviewer is outlining the approach taken by Hoopes by explaining that the book is primarily a series of biographical sketches of key thinkers.

title: Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "This is where Hoopes’ credibility wanes; he is prone to unsupported generalisations and seems to have his own agenda, ultimately promoting a theory of the proper role of management that is both ill-defined and outside the scope of his biographical treatments."
Why: Option A restates this as relying on unsupported generalisations rather than providing adequate evidence to validate his arguments.

title: Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The husband-and-wife team Frank and Lillian Gilbreth, and Henry Gantt (who advocated bonus pay, rather than threats, as a motivational tool), either tried to soften Taylor’s tactics or disdained them altogether, while trying to combine efficient processes with consideration for the workers."
Why: Option B restates this by showing that they had a more sympathetic approach to the workers through consideration for them and softening harsh tactics.

title: Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Perhaps more than any other business management guru, she added new, substantive theories, which are still reflected in management practice today."
Why: Option A restates this by noting that she made a significant contribution to the development of management theory through her new and substantive theories.

title: Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Bottom-up management, he argues, is even worse than top-down; rather than limiting the potential abuses of managerial power, it cloaks such abuses in a false morality."
Why: The passage states that bottom-up management "cloaks such abuses", meaning it is just as "abusive" as top-down management.

title: Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "He also argues that Americans believe in sociopolitical democracy but that most workplaces lack such democracy."
Why: The summary uses "democratic" to reflect the passage's mention that workplaces lack "sociopolitical democracy" and working people do not experience it.

title: Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "He claims that top-down workplace hierarchies produce better results than democratic organisational structures and concludes that people need to accept that top-down management power is necessary to some degree, though its importance is overstated by the management gurus."
Why: The passage notes that top-down structures "produce better results", which means they are more "successful" in terms of outcome.

title: Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "He claims that top-down workplace hierarchies produce better results than democratic organisational structures and concludes that people need to accept that top-down management power is necessary to some degree, though its importance is overstated by the management gurus."
Why: The passage states that the gurus overstate the "importance" of top-down power, which matches the option "significant".

title: Book Review: False Prophets: The Gurus Who Created Modern Management and Why Their Ideas Are Bad for Business Today by James Hoopes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Instead, he merely draws his own personal conclusions based on the anecdotes and observations contained in his biographical sketches."
Why: Drawing personal conclusions based on anecdotes instead of evidence means his information is entirely "subjective".

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Yet sundews, he observed, ignored raindrops."
Why: The notes state that Darwin understood why the plant did not respond to something, and the passage confirms he noticed sundews ignored raindrops to avoid false alarms.

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "He showed that when one of its leaves snapped shut, it formed itself into a temporary ‘stomach’, secreting enzymes that could dissolve the prey."
Why: The summary explains that the leaves act like a temporary structure for digestion, which the passage explicitly identifies as a "stomach".

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Volkov’s experiments reveal that the electric charge travels down fluid-filled tunnels in a leaf, which opens up pores in cell membranes."
Why: The notes describe the electric charge opening something in the cell walls, and the passage states that this opens "pores" in the cell membranes.

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "The cells in the bladder then begin to pump water out again, creating a new vacuum."
Why: The notes explain that pumping water out of the bladder cells builds something up inside, which the passage refers to as a "vacuum".

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Some of the largest have pitchers up to 30 cm deep and can consume whole frogs unlucky enough to fall into them."
Why: The notes ask what large pitcher plants can capture and eat, and the passage states they can consume "frogs".

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "Carnivorous plants clearly benefit from eating animals; when scientists feed pitcher plants extra bugs, the plants get bigger."
Why: The passage states that feeding pitcher plants extra bugs makes them bigger, which directly matches the statement that they increase in size after eating insects.

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "Carnivorous plants, however, take nitrogen and phosphorus from the flesh in order to build light-harvesting enzymes."
Why: The statement says they produce light-harvesting enzymes with nutrients extracted from animals, which is a direct paraphrase of taking nitrogen and phosphorus (nutrients) from flesh to build those enzymes.

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "A pitcher or a flytrap is not very good at photosynthesis because, unlike plants with ordinary leaves, they do not have flat solar panels that can absorb lots of sunlight."
Why: The passage explicitly states that pitcher plants and flytraps are not very good at photosynthesis compared to ordinary leaves, directly contradicting the claim that they are more efficient.

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "The poor soil of bogs and swamps, where many carnivorous plants grow, offers little nitrogen and phosphorus, so carnivorous plants enjoy an advantage there over ‘conventional’ plants."
Why: The passage compares carnivorous plants to conventional plants in bogs and swamps, but it never compares Venus flytraps to *other* carnivorous plants in terms of soil adaptation.

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "Also, bogs are often flooded with sunshine, so even an inefficient carnivorous plant can carry out enough photosynthesis to survive."
Why: The passage states that bogs are often flooded with sunshine, which contradicts the statement that they find it difficult to photosynthesise due to a lack of sunlight.

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 11
Quote: "Chemical fertilizers used in agriculture and pollution from power plants are adding extra nitrogen to many bogs in North America."
Why: While the passage mentions agricultural fertilizers adding nitrogen to bogs, it is completely silent on whether scientists have campaigned to reduce this nitrogen release.

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 11
Quote: "The black market trade in exotic carnivorous plants is strong, but even if this can be prevented, carnivorous plants will continue to suffer from other dangers."
Why: The passage confirms a strong black market trade in exotic carnivorous plants, which directly supports the statement that a lot of them are sold illegally.

title: Carnivorous Plants
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 11
Quote: "The suppression of wildfires by government agencies allows other plants to grow quickly and outcompete the Venus flytraps."
Why: The passage states that wildfire suppression helps other plants outcompete Venus flytraps, meaning preventing wildfires is harmful rather than beneficial to them.

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Art and music have flourished in those periods of history, and those parts of society, in which the luxury of free time and material wealth has allowed such a culture to take precedence over more material matters."
Why: This sentence explains that art and music only thrive when basic material demands are met; conversely, a focus on survival and basic needs limits where and when these cultural practices can happen, matching heading III.

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "It was until the 18th century that this situation changed to any great extent, and the rise of an economically independent middle class meant that concert going became a public activity for anyone who cared to buy a ticket."
Why: The paragraph describes how the 18th century brought the rise of public concerts and ticket-buying audiences, meaning a much wider range of people gained access to live music (heading II).

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "But nothing has changed music over the last century more radically than the invention and dissemination of recording technologies."
Why: The passage details a series of technological developments—from Edison's phonograph and wax cylinders to vinyl, CDs, digital MP3 files, and phones—that brought recorded music to an increasingly wide audience, matching heading V.

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "Even when music became professionalized, people who wanted to listen to music went to a specific venue, at a specific time, to hear musicians create a one-off event."
Why: This sums up the core theme of the paragraph: before recording technologies existed, listening to music was strictly limited to attending live performances, which corresponds to heading VI.

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 11
Quote: "As a consequence, all music, classical music included, can become any person's soundtrack for activities such as commuting, exercising or shopping."
Why: The paragraph explains that digital technology frees music from specific venues and occasions, allowing people to enjoy it in a large variety of everyday situations (heading I).

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 13
Quote: "Put very simply, the history of classical music, in all its varied forms, is the history of a tradition that grew out of the possibilities of musical notation."
Why: This concluding sentence ties together the entire paragraph, explaining how classical music has managed to survive and remain viable for centuries through the system of written notation (heading VII).

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Yet now, people have more music stored on their phones or computers — which they can call up with the touch of a finger — than would have been contained on all the metres of library shelves of a proud “record collector” of the 20th century."
Why: This matches the idea that electronic storage (phones or computers) allows people to keep a vast amount of music compared to past collections.

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "From the mid-1980s onwards, the vinyl disc gradually gave way to the new technology of the CD, but just a decade later, the digital MP file was already displacing the CD as the favoured way to produce recorded music."
Why: This shows the CD was popular for a relatively brief period, lasting only about a decade before being displaced by digital MP3 files.

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 13
Quote: "The first attempts to notate music were intended to help them remember these."
Why: This matches the statement that musical notation was originally designed as a memory aid.

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 13
Quote: "Put very simply, the history of classical music, in all its varied forms, is the history of a tradition that grew out of the possibilities of musical notation."
Why: This supports the idea that classical music relies fundamentally on musical notation to survive and develop over time.

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "It is no longer restricted to a particular audience or group of musicians."
Why: The text states that music is no longer restricted to a particular audience, which matches the summary's gap requiring the specific group associated with it.

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 11
Quote: "One of its distinctive aspects — a performance defined by concert halls and opera houses — is dissolved by digital recording formats."
Why: The summary mentions venues like opera houses where concerts are performed, and the text specifically pairs them with "concert halls" (shortened to "halls" in the text context).

title: Classical music over the centuries
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 11
Quote: "As a consequence, all music, classical music included, can become any person's soundtrack for activities such as commuting, exercising or shopping."
Why: The passage explains that music can become a person's "soundtrack" for daily activities, directly fitting the gap about treating music as a background accompaniment.

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "After consulting with companies who were interested in designing for the Nintendo DS, we
decided on three key objectives for our initial exploratory project: understand preschoolers
abilities in the context of handheld system game play; understand how preschoolers interact
with the Nintendo DS, specifically how they handle the various forms of play and game
mechanics offered by the games currently on the market for this system; and understand the
expectations of their parents with regard to handheld systems."
Why: The prompt asks for what needs to be determined regarding preschool children, matching the text's objective to "understand preschoolers abilities".

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "After consulting with companies who were interested in designing for the Nintendo DS, we
decided on three key objectives for our initial exploratory project: understand preschoolers
abilities in the context of handheld system game play; understand how preschoolers interact
with the Nintendo DS, specifically how they handle the various forms of play and game
mechanics offered by the games currently on the market for this system; and understand the
expectations of their parents with regard to handheld systems."
Why: The prompt asks to investigate the attitudes of preschoolers' ___, matching the text's objective to "understand the expectations of their parents".

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The research team began by
conducting 26 in-home interviews with children in three markets across the US (West coast
urban/suburban: Midwest suburban/rural; and East coast urban/suburban)."
Why: The prompt refers to children from different US ___, which matches the text stating they were from "three markets across the US".

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "In addition, because previous research we conducted
had shown the effects of school-age siblings on game play (demonstrated, for example, by
more advanced motor coordination when using a computer mouse), a combination of
households was recruited which had preschoolers with and without school-age siblings."
Why: The summary notes that some children had older ___, which corresponds to the passage mentioning households with and without "school-age siblings".

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "In
addition, in order to understand both experienced preschool users of the system and those
who were new to video games, we split the sample so that thirteen families owned at least
one Nintendo DS and thirteen did not."
Why: The note contrasts "new" players with another type, and the text refers directly to "experienced" preschool users.

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "From the parents and any older siblings
that were available, we found out, where relevant, the purchase decisions surrounding game
systems in the household; the family's typical game play habits; levels of parental supervision
with regard to gaming; and favorite games played by various family members."
Why: "Levels of parental supervision" directly matches how far mothers or fathers controlled their children's game playing.

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Because these
interviews were in-home, we were also able to understand the gaming culture in these
homes: what types of spaces (communal or private) were used for game play; how the
systems were set up; where the handheld play occurred in the house; and the number and
type of games and game systems owned."
Why: While the passage mentions understanding which spaces in the house were used for game play, it never states whether researchers were given free access to *all* parts of the subjects' houses.

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "It was chosen because it was one of the few games on
the market with characters that all of this young age group really liked."
Why: The game having characters that the young age group really liked shows that the researchers regarded it as likely to appeal to preschoolers.

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Also, it incorporated a
large variety of operating techniques that highlighted the uniqueness of the Nintendo DS
system, including blowing or singing into the microphone."
Why: The passage states the game used techniques like blowing or singing into the microphone, which contradicts the claim that it is operated entirely by hand controls.

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "After reviewing the results inhouse and discussing the implications for game design, we then outlined our needs to a firm
specializing in children's games."
Why: The flow-chart item mentions presenting requirements to a "specialist ___", and the text confirms they outlined their needs to a "firm" specializing in children's games.

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "Whenever we developed new game mechanics, we brought preschoolers into our lab to try
them, so we could assess not only their simplicity, but also how engaging they were."
Why: The flow-chart states that mechanics were assessed for interest and another quality, which matches "simplicity" tested for how simple the mechanics were.

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "Once a
full version of the Nintendo DS games was ready, we went back into the field and tested with
a dozen preschoolers, to make sure that each element of the games worked for the children,
and that overall the games were understandable and enjoyable for them."
Why: The flow-chart refers to "a ___ of each game trialled with twelve children", and the text describes testing a "full version" with a dozen (twelve) preschoolers.

title: Computer Games for Preschoolers: Nintendo's Research and Design Process
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "We also got feedback on what their siblings and parents thought about the games with regard
to appropriateness, engagement, and purchase-intent."
Why: The final step in the flow-chart involves the collection of opinions from family members, which the passage explicitly refers to as "feedback" from parents and siblings.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "However, although discussion-based classes at university level can be a catalyst for developing students' thinking skills, they are often a source of frustration for staff and students."
Why: This sentence introduces the dual nature of class discussions—their positive value contrasted with the frustration they cause—which aligns with the conflicting evidence about their benefits.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Inadequate preparation is another common reason for lack of student participation."
Why: The paragraph outlines specific causes for why students fail to engage, such as received knowledge, fear of embarrassment, and inadequate preparation, matching the reasons for a lack of involvement.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "The attitude of the instructor has been described as instrumental in shaping a successful discussion (VanDeWeghe, 2003)."
Why: The entire paragraph details how specific teacher behaviours (such as open-mindedness, avoiding sarcasm, and giving waiting time) directly affect the quality of classroom discussions.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "One of the main challenges of a discussion class is ensuring a common base of knowledge."
Why: The paragraph explains both student preparation (mastering factual knowledge) and instructor actions (asking challenging, higher-order questions) required to generate effective, subject-centred discussions at the appropriate level.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Course assignments foster discussion by increasing the likelihood that students have the foundation to make meaningful contributions."
Why: The paragraph discusses how assessment methods like tests, daily quizzes, and response papers provide incentives and evaluation practices that shape and promote student participation.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "The classroom setting and atmosphere can either inhibit or enhance the sense of a learning community."
Why: The paragraph focuses on how physical layout adjustments, such as arranging chairs in a circle and using name cards, influence the success and quality of classroom interactions.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Daily quizzes and journals provide more immediate incentives than having several tests over the course of the semester."
Why: The statement says frequent testing improves learning, and the passage links daily quizzes (frequent tests) to providing incentives and fostering increased analytical skills.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "This is a learned behaviour for which students are often rewarded; many students report earning outstanding grades in classes that offer no opportunity or incentive for speaking (Belenky et al., 1986)."
Why: The statement mentions getting high marks despite no participation, which matches Belenky et al.'s finding that students earn outstanding grades in classes offering no opportunity or incentive to speak.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "A common complaint from professors in universities is that class discussions simply do not work because students are unable to participate in them effectively (McKeachie, 1999)."
Why: The statement about instructors frequently reporting unsuccessful discussions is a direct restatement of McKeachie's note on professors complaining that discussions do not work.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Instructors who display open-mindedness, enthusiasm, passion, humour, and who hold high expectations while allowing students the opportunity to make and learn from mistakes appear to foster high-quality discussion."
Why: The summary states that treating something as "learning opportunities" improves discussion; the passage specifies that allowing students to "make and learn from mistakes" fosters high-quality discussion.

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Instructors can reinforce and support student participation by writing comments up on the board, correcting misinformation or incomplete ideas with dignity, and being able to refer to students by their names."
Why: The summary mentions recording students' ideas for everyone to see, which corresponds to the passage's mention of "writing comments up on the board".

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Instructors can reinforce and support student participation by writing comments up on the board, correcting misinformation or incomplete ideas with dignity, and being able to refer to students by their names."
Why: The summary notes that demonstrating familiarity with students is motivating, and the passage explains this is done by being able to refer to them by their "names".

title: Creating Meaningful Discussions in the Classroom
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "If a question is challenging, it will take students time to formulate meaningful responses; a pause of as long as 30 seconds can stimulate thoughtful discussion (McKeachie, 1999)."
Why: The summary refers to permitting a lengthy period after asking a question, which matches the passage's mention of a "pause".

title: Decision Fatigue
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "The sugary lemonade provided a burst of glucose, the effects of which could be observed immediately in the lab; the sugarless sweeteners tasted similar but did not contain the glucose."
Why: This sentence explains how the researchers used two substances (sugary lemonade and sugarless sweeteners) that tasted alike but yielded different results regarding willpower.

title: Decision Fatigue
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "When they tried to resist the urge to cry during a sad movie, afterwards they gave up more quickly on tasks requiring self-discipline, such as working on a geometry puzzle."
Why: Controlling emotions while watching a sad movie is an example of controlling emotions during an upsetting viewing, which led to giving up quickly (lack of perseverance) on a geometry puzzle.

title: Decision Fatigue
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "If a decision must be made late in the afternoon or in the evening, they know not to do it on an empty stomach."
Why: This advice explains why eating something (avoiding an empty stomach) is necessary when making late-day decisions.

title: Decision Fatigue
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "However, some brain researchers had reservations about the glucose connection."
Why: This introduces Todd Heatherton and other researchers who initially doubted or had reservations about how glucose levels could cause ego depletion.

title: Decision Fatigue
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "Decision fatigue leaves people vulnerable to marketers who know how to time their sales, as Jonathan Levav demonstrated."
Why: The passage describes how Jonathan Levav experienced decision fatigue while buying a wedding suit, and then used that personal experience to conduct further research at car dealerships.

title: Decision Fatigue
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "No matter how rational people try to be, they can’t make decision after decision without paying a biological price."
Why: The text states that no matter how "rational" people try to be, they cannot avoid paying a biological price when making continuous decisions.

title: Decision Fatigue
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "This ‘decision fatigue’ is different from ordinary physical fatigue, people are not conscious of being tired, but nevertheless they are low on energy."
Why: The summary notes that people are not aware of how "tired" they are despite being low on energy, matching the text's reference to not being conscious of being tired.

title: Decision Fatigue
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "The more choices one makes throughout the day, the harder it becomes for the brain, and eventually it looks for shortcuts: either to act impulsively instead of expending the energy to think through the possible results, or the ultimate energy saver: do nothing."
Why: The passage explains that the brain eventually looks for "shortcuts" to save energy when it becomes too hard to make more choices.

title: Decision Fatigue
