title: Improving Patient Safety
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Two or three of these are then tested on a consumer group."
Why: The passage mentions that over-the-counter designs are commissioned from an "external design team" who come up with the designs after the initial brief.

title: Improving Patient Safety
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Two or three of these are then tested on a consumer group."
Why: The summary states that selected designs are shown to consumers, which matches the text's reference to testing them on a "consumer group."

title: Improving Patient Safety
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "In contrast, most designs for prescription-only products are created in-house."
Why: For prescription-only drugs, the design is created internally by the company's "in-house design team."

title: Improving Patient Safety
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "In some cases, this may simply involve the company's design team applying the house design and then handing it over to design engineers rather than testing the design on a consumer group."
Why: The passage explicitly states that the design is subsequently handed over to "design engineers."

title: Improving Patient Safety
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Investigations following this tragedy attributed some blame to the poor choice of typescript used on the drug container."
Why: The question asks about the design consideration that caused a drug to be given incorrectly in an accident; option D restates this as the "style of print", which paraphrases "poor choice of typescript".

title: Improving Patient Safety
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 14
Quote: "One argument is that if all packaging was white with black lettering, people would have no choice but to read every box carefully."
Why: The question asks what some people say about using only black and white on packaging; option D restates this as "People would pay more attention to label information," which paraphrases having "no choice but to read every box carefully".

title: Improving Patient Safety
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 16
Quote: "On a positive note, a recent innovation exhibition revealed several new designs."
Why: The question asks why the writer mentions 'the popper' and 'Pluspoint'; option D restates this by showing "that progress is being made in pharmaceutical packaging design", reflecting the positive tone regarding new innovations.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "By letting spectators share in the motions of victory, they also allow us to share in their feelings."
Why: The passage explains that mirror neurons are directly connected to the amygdala (an emotional region), allowing spectators to share in the feelings of athletes, which explains why watching sport is emotionally satisfying.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "To the novice, however, the skill of casting a smooth arc with a lop-side metal stick is virtually impossible."
Why: The text contrasts experts with novices, explaining that novices swing with their consciousness using a different part of the brain rather than having the motor actions embedded in their premotor cortex, which is why sporting tasks feel so difficult for beginners.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "The best athletes are those with a premotor cortex capable of imagining the movements of victory, together with the physical properties to make those movements real."
Why: The question asks for a factor that combines with mirroring to achieve sporting excellence; the text identifies this combination as the mental ability (premotor cortex imagination) alongside the "physical properties to make those movements real."

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Humans have an even more elaborate mirror neuron system."
Why: This sentence directly compares the mirror neuron systems of humans and animals (previously discussed in relation to monkeys), noting that the human system is "more elaborate."

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "This phenomenon of neural mirroring was first discovered in 1954, when two French physiologists, Gastaut and Berf, found that the brains of humans vibrate with two distinct wavelengths, alpha and mu."
Why: The passage explicitly states that neural mirroring brain activity was first discovered in 1954 by two French physiologists observing alpha and mu wavelengths.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "It turns out that watching a great golfer makes us better golfers, and watching a great sprinter actually makes us run faster."
Why: This statement directly links the observation of sports (watching a great golfer or sprinter) to an improvement in performance (becoming better golfers or running faster).

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Just as there are grammars of movement."
Why: Option B restates this as "a pattern of connected cells" because the text immediately refers to these as "networks of cells" that store motor actions.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "He hits the ball with the tranquility of his perfected autopilot."
Why: Option C restates this as "without conscious thought" because an autopilot performs actions automatically rather than relying on conscious effort.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Rather, we watch sport for the feeling, the human drama."
Why: Option A restates this as "experience strong positive emotions" because the passage explains that watching sports allows us to share in feelings like victory and emotion connected to the amygdala.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "This is because most novices swing with their consciousness, using an area of the brain next to the premotor cortex."
Why: The writer states that beginners swing "with their consciousness," which directly supports the idea that inexpert players are overly aware of what they are doing.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Humans have an even more elaborate mirror neuron system."
Why: The statement claims that monkeys have a more complex system, but the writer states the exact opposite: humans have the more elaborate mirror neuron system.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "If we are staring at a photograph, a fixed image of a runner mid-stride, our mirror neurons are totally silent."
Why: The question claims photographs can activate these neurons, but the writer states directly that mirror neurons are "totally silent" when looking at a photograph.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "This phenomenon of neural mirroring was first discovered in 1954, when two French physiologists, Gastaut and Berf, found that the brains of humans vibrate with two distinct wavelengths, alpha and mu."
Why: The text mentions that Gastaut and Berf were French physiologists who discovered neural wavelengths, but it never states whether or not they were also sports players.

title: Inside the Mind of a Fan
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "It is active when your bodies are still and disappears whenever you do something active, like playing a sport or changing the TV channel."
Why: The writer explains that the mu system "disappears" (meaning it is inactive or at rest) whenever you do something active, matching the statement that it is at rest during activity.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "However, exciting new research on a number of animals, particularly birds, has called into question the uniqueness of these traits, forcing us to reconsider this opinion."
Why: This heading fits because the paragraph discusses how new discoveries about birds challenge the long-held belief that intelligence and traits like tool use are exclusively human.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "At least three Australian bird species make tools similar to those of the woodpecker finch, and when white-winged choughs come across shellfish they have been known to use rocks as hammers to crack open the recalcitrant shells."
Why: This section lists various examples of different bird species—such as Australian birds, white-winged choughs, and black kites—using tools in creative ways.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "The predominant explanation is based on the proverb that 'necessity is the mother of invention'."
Why: This paragraph explains the evolutionary theory that birds develop intelligence and tool-making abilities as a survival mechanism to overcome challenging environments and find food.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "New Caledonian crows boast many different tools in their tool kit."
Why: The heading is correct because the paragraph focuses entirely on one specific species—the New Caledonian crow—and describes the multiple types of tools it makes and uses.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "The team uncovered a clear relationship: birds with relatively large forebrains are able to invent fresh solutions to ecological challenges, and to exploit the discoveries and inventions of others, more often than birds with relatively small forebrains."
Why: This paragraph provides physiological and scientific evidence—specifically brain size data collected by biologists—to link brain structure directly to birds' problem-solving intelligence.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Intelligence in birds may also arise as a result of selection to overcome the dynamic challenges of communal living."
Why: This matches the theory that high cognitive abilities evolve in social animals as a way to handle the competition and complex dynamics of living together in groups.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "For example, when an adult is watching, a young chough will place some food in the mouth of a hungry chick - but it does not release the food."
Why: The paragraph illustrates how young white-winged choughs deceive adults by pretending to feed chicks or help out only when they are being watched in order to protect their social status.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "The crows carry their favourite tool from one foraging site to the next."
Why: "carry their favourite tool" matches the idea of "keeping tools that they like to use".

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "The bird then feasts on the small animals that flee from the subsequent fire."
Why: Frightening animals out by dropping a smouldering stick to start a fire matches drawing out prey by frightening it.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "and when white-winged choughs come across shellfish they have been known to use rocks as hammers to crack open the recalcitrant shells."
Why: Using rocks to crack open shells corresponds to using tools to remove the outer covering from food.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "For example, black kites have been reported dropping bait into lakes to bring fish to the surface of the water, thereby making them easier to catch."
Why: Dropping bait into water to bring fish to the surface is an example of using food to attract prey.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "Recently, New Caledonian crows were observed moulding a piece of wire, something they had never seen before, into a hook and then using it to retrieve food."
Why: Moulding a piece of wire that they had never seen before matches the use of unfamiliar materials to make tools.

title: Intelligent behavior in birds
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "Interestingly, it is more likely to preen the chicks if another bird can see it do so."
Why: Preening the chicks more when another bird is watching means they engage in the activity for the benefit of observers.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "It was a shift comparable to the way modern anthropology displaced stories of primitive tribes being 'noble savages' and 'cannibals'."
Why: Option B restates this as "how Piaget's work represents a crucial turning-point in our approach to education" by comparing it to a major paradigm shift in anthropology that changed how people were viewed.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Classifying them as 'true' or 'false' misses the point and shows a lack of respect for the child."
Why: Option D restates this as "The factual accuracy of what children say is of minor significance" because judging their answers simply as right or wrong ("true or false") misses what is truly important about their reasoning.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "If their theories are always greeted by 'Nice try, but this is how it really is...' they might give up after a while on making theories."
Why: Option B restates this as "maintaining children's confidence in their ability to interpret the world" by showing that constantly correcting children can discourage them from continuing to create their own theories.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Disciples of Piaget have a tolerance for—indeed a fascination with—children’s primitive laws of physics: that things disappear when they are out of sight; that the moon and the sun follow you around; that big things float and small things sink."
Why: Option C restates this as "Even apparently irrational ideas can be worthy of interest" because people who follow Piaget are fascinated by and tolerate these basic, seemingly illogical beliefs children hold.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "Since Piaget, the territory has been widely colonised by those who write about women's ways of knowing, Afrocentric ways of knowing, even the computer's ways of knowing."
Why: Option C restates this as "outline Piaget's contribution to a range of scientific fields" by showing how his work on epistemology expanded into various areas like artificial intelligence, information processing, and different cultural perspectives.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "After thousands of interactions with young people often barely old enough to talk, Piaget began to suspect that behind their cute and seemingly irrational utterances were thought processes that had their own kind of order and their own special logic."
Why: The passage states that children's thinking has "their own special logic," which means their mental processes are far more "logical" than they might appear.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "He has been revered by generations of teachers inspired by the belief that children are not empty vessels to be filled with knowledge (as traditional pedagogical theory had it) but active builders of knowledge—little scientists who are constantly creating and testing their own hypotheses about the world."
Why: The passage mentions that children are "creating and testing their own hypotheses," which is a direct paraphrase of trying out their own "theories" about the world.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "And though he may not be as famous as Sigmund Freud or even B F Skinner, his influence on psychology may be longer lasting."
Why: The passage explicitly compares his lasting influence to other pioneers in "psychology," matching the summary's mention of this discipline.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "In the past decade, Piaget has been vigorously challenged by the current fashion of viewing knowledge as an intrinsic property of the brain."
Why: The summary refers to the current view associating knowledge with the "brain," which directly mirrors the passage stating that knowledge is viewed as "an intrinsic property of the brain."

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Although every teacher in training still memorises Piaget’s successive stages of childhood development, the greater part of Piaget’s work is less well known, perhaps because schools of education regard it as ‘too deep’ for teachers."
Why: The passage notes that every "teacher" in training memorises his stages and that his work is studied by those training to be educators, matching the professional development of "teachers."

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In 1920, while doing research in a child-psychology laboratory in Paris, Piaget noticed that children of the same age made similar errors on intelligence tests."
Why: The passage mentions he did research in Paris and noticed children's errors, but it never states whether his research techniques were "innovative," making this NOT GIVEN.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Piaget was not an educator and never laid down rules about how to intervene in such situations."
Why: The statement claims Piaget gave "clear guidelines" (rules), but the writer explicitly states he "never laid down rules about how to intervene," which directly contradicts the question.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "His real interest was epistemology—the theory of knowledge—which, like physics, was considered a branch of philosophy until Piaget came along and made it a science."
Why: The writer claims Piaget transformed epistemology from a branch of philosophy into a science, which means he made a significant contribution to the field.

title: Jean Piaget 1896-1980
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "Whether this has in fact led to deeper understanding remains, like everything about Piaget, controversial."
Why: The writer notes that understanding the nature of knowledge through Piaget's work remains controversial and leaves a massive gap between babies and adults, supporting the idea that we still have much to learn.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Tough new rules for new developments mean that drains will be prevented from becoming overloaded after heavy rains."
Why: "Tough new rules" corresponds to "legislation", and "new developments" with architectural/building designers relates to improving water use.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "The aim was partly to improve navigation, and partly to speed floodwaters out of Alps and down to the North Sea."
Why: This sentence directly gives the "two reasons" (improve navigation, speed floodwaters) for why the Rhine was isolated from its plain.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Back in the days when rivers took a winding path to the sea, floodwaters lost force and volume while meandering across flood plains and inland deltas, but today the water tends to have a direct passage to the sea."
Why: It explains how meandering across flood plains caused waters to lose force and volume in the past, thus assisting flood control.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "The engineers calculate that the restored flood plain of the Drava River can now store up to 10 million cubic metres of floodwater, and slow down storm surges coming out of the Alps by more than an hour, protecting towns not only in Austria, but as far downstream as Slovenia and Croatia."
Why: This describes flood control on the Drava River that protects towns across three countries: Austria, Slovenia, and Croatia.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Since that time, the Dutch have broken one of their most enduring national stereotypes by allowing engineers to punch holes in dykes."
Why: Punching holes in dykes refers to destroying one of their characteristic national features (since dykes are a typical Dutch stereotype associated with water control).

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "It may sound expensive, until we realise how much is spent trying to drain cities and protect areas from flooding, and bow little this method achieves."
Why: This comment compares the high cost and low achievement of traditional methods with the new approach, addressing cost effectiveness.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "They are reviving river bends and marshes to curb the flow, and even plugging city drains to encourage floodwater to use other means to go underground."
Why: Reviving river bends and marshes to "curb the flow" directly matches the idea of slowing the movement of water to the sea.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "They plan to return up to a sixth of the country to its former waterlogged state in order to better protect the rest."
Why: Returning a part of the country to a waterlogged state means those areas of land will be given over to water, matching the loss of land for human use.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "Recently, winter floods on the rivers of central Europe have been among the worst for 600 to 700 years, and dams and dykes (protective sea walls) have failed to solve the problem."
Why: The sentence in the text states that floods have recently occurred in "central Europe", which matches the missing location in the gapped sentence.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "The same thing has happened in the US on the Mississippi river, which drains the world’s second largest river catchment into the Gulf of Mexico."
Why: The text links the Rhine's problems to the "Mississippi" river, which experienced similar issues with water control despite engineering efforts.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "To help keep London's feet dry, the UK Environment Agency is reflooding 10 square kilometres of the ancient flood plain of the River Thames outside Oxford."
Why: The passage explains that reflooding an area near Oxford is done "To help keep London's feet dry", meaning it protects the city of London.

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "A new breed of ‘soft engineers’ wants cities to porous, Berlin is one place where this is being done."
Why: The question asks for the name given to planners who want water to pass more freely through city surfaces; the text identifies them as "soft engineers".

title: Keeping the water away
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "Los Angeles has recently launched a new scheme to utilise floodwater in the Sun Valley section of the city."
Why: The gapped summary asks for a proposal regarding part of the city of "Los Angeles", referring to the new scheme launched in the Sun Valley section.

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "However, their insidious creep can have serious consequences if there is an oil installation or a railway line in their path."
Why: This sentence explains how the slow-moving dunes pose a danger to industrial structures and transport links, which matches heading IV ("A potential threat to industry and communications").

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Only around 20% of that is sand-covered, however, and over half of that is classified as ‘linear’ sand dunes."
Why: The paragraph details linear sand dunes, noting that they make up over half of the sand-covered desert, which corresponds to heading VIII ("The commonest type of dune").

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "‘Barchan dunes only tend to form where you have one-directional winds on the edge of sandy deserts near coastal areas,’ says Giles Wiggs, a geomorphologist at Oxford University, who has been studying the formation and movement of sand dunes for more than a decade."
Why: The quotation outlines the precise environmental conditions required for barchan dunes to form, matching heading VI ("Needing a specific combination of conditions").

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "Eventually, it reappears at the back of the due, the whole thin creeps in the direction of the prevailing wind."
Why: This traces the step-by-step movement of sand grains in a loop that keeps the dune shifting forward, illustrating heading VII ("A continuous cycle").

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Even when two dunes collide, they quickly take on their distinctive shapes again."
Why: This statement describes how dunes merge and regain their original forms, directly reflecting heading V ("Dunes coming together and re-forming").

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "Local legends attributed the sounds to dangerous spirits which were trying to trop unwary travellers."
Why: The paragraph contrasts old myths about spirits with a scientific explanation of the singing dunes, fitting heading IX ("Old superstitions demystified").

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "What really surprised the scientists, however, was that they were able to take samples of the singing sand back to France and replicate the sound at ENS, proving that it’s the sand, not the dune shape, well- rounded from years of striking each other, and that the variations in size affect the tone."
Why: The text details how researchers successfully duplicated the sound using sand samples in a facility, which matches heading II ("Recreating the process in a laboratory").

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "These form in a long curving wave, as a result of wind blowing strongly from several quarters, flipping them from side to side."
Why: The passage states that linear dunes form in a "long curving wave," and option C restates this as developing in a recognizable shape.

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "That question was first answered in the mid-20th century by British explorer Ralph Alger Bagnold, and his answer hinges on the fact tat dunes aren’t solid, but granular."
Why: Bagnold found that movement happens because dunes are made of separate grains rather than being solid, which option C paraphrases as their particular composition.

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "‘Interestingly the dune can regulate its own shape, and maintain it as it moves.’"
Why: Dr Douady compares them to living organisms because they keep their outline the same even while moving, which option C restates as maintaining an outline after a period of movement.

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "They are known as ‘barchans’: heavy, crescent-shaped sand piles with a ridged crest and two elongated arms, one curving away to either side."
Why: The text states that the singing dunes belong to this specific category of moving dunes, which are introduced as "barchans".

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "proving that it’s the sand, not the dune shape, well- rounded from years of striking each other, and that the variations in size affect the tone."
Why: The summary states that individual grains share a similar physical characteristic, which corresponds to them being "well- rounded" in the text.

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "and that the variations in size affect the tone."
Why: The text explicitly links the different dimensions (sizes) of the grains to the changes in the "tone" of the sound produced.

title: Living dunes
explanation:
Where: Paragraph G
Quote: "Crucially, the grains are coated with a special veneer, which Douady calls ‘desert glaze,’ made from a precise combination of minerals from surrounding rocks including iron, aluminium, manganese, silicon and calcium."
Why: The summary requires the substance covering each grain, and the text identifies this as a combination of "minerals".

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "In terms of access, the literature suggests that most children, even at quite a young age, already possess the competencies needed to gain access to media content: they are quite skilled at using the available technologies and are also able to use the associated software."
Why: The heading in the notes is "having [access] to communications", which directly matches the first dimension discussed in the text ("In terms of access").

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "The large majority of children show some awareness of risks relating to giving personal information, such as contact details, on the internet, although they are less aware of financial dangers such as those relating to credit card use or communication of banking details."
Why: The note mentions children lacking awareness of certain risks regarding internet use; the text contrasts personal information risks with "financial dangers" (credit cards and banking details).

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In terms of understanding, most of the research literature relates to the development of children's understanding of television, rather than of other media such as the internet."
Why: The note states that research has focused on children and a specific medium rather than alternatives, and the text confirms this was "television".

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "This literature suggests that children's awareness of areas such as the difference between representation and reality, and the persuasive role of advertising, develops both as a function of their increasing knowledge of the world, and as a result of their broader cognitive development."
Why: The note explains that children's awareness grows alongside their knowledge of the world and their "cognitive development", which is taken directly from the passage.

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Children also learn to cope with potentially unwanted or upsetting emotional responses, and to form critical judgments about areas such as television violence, by employing forms of media literacy."
Why: The note says children use media literacy to cope with negative responses and to make "critical judgments", matching the exact phrase from the text.

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "By contrast, when it comes to creativity, there has been less academic research relating to the 'older' media such as video and analogue radio than to the new media."
Why: The note states that most research on creating communications has focused on "new media", contrasting with older media like video and analogue radio.

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Research here suggests that there is considerable potential for media to be used as a means of self-expression, not least by socially disadvantaged groups; that creative involvement in media production (particularly in the context of education) can make an important contribution to the development of critical understanding; and that new media such as online gaming and mobile telephony provide possibilities for new forms of interaction."
Why: The note lists the uses of new media, including self-expression, the development of understanding, and "interaction" (derived from "new forms of interaction").

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Less is known about other potential barriers such as disability, or about the role of individual dispositions or motivations."
Why: The statement claims that "considerable research has been done" on disability, which directly contradicts the passage stating that "less is known" about it.

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "It is important to recognize that such barriers may affect the quality of media use as well as the quantity - for example, in terms of the available functionality of the technology, the location or level of support for use."
Why: The passage states that the "level of support for use" is an example of a barrier that can affect the quality of media use, which matches the statement that parental support affects quality.

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "These include specific media, such as radio, mobile phones and online gaming, and particular population groups, such as younger children, those with disabilities, and ethnic minority groups."
Why: While the passage mentions that younger children and mobile phones are gaps in the literature requiring more research, it gives no information about whether young children are "badly affected" by using them.

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "By contrast, when it comes to creativity, there has been less academic research relating to the 'older' media such as video and analogue radio than to the new media."
Why: The text highlights that research into 'understanding' is well-documented compared to the lesser amount of research regarding 'creativity', making the statement true.

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "In terms of methodology, the review finds that a great deal of research in the field is based on self-reporting, and recommends that there should be more observational studies that explore how media literacy is used in everyday life."
Why: The statement claims that "too many observational studies have been conducted", whereas the passage actually recommends that there should be "more observational studies."

title: Media literacy
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "The nature and extent of the media literacy that individuals develop depends very much on the purposes for which they use the media in the first place."
Why: The passage explains that the media literacy someone develops depends on their "purposes" for using the media, which means the reasons a person has for using media affect their media literacy.

title: Mirrors clear
explanation:

title: Surviving city life

title: The ability to communicate using language

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

Why: The paragraph outlines how storylines and Hollywood structures are used in games to maintain player loyalty and pacing, which matches the heading about why stories are included in games.

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

title: The attraction of video games
explanation:

Why: The passage notes that the opening levels (the first part) are "short", and later states that a "short final act" is often used, meaning both the first and last parts are short.

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:

Why: The passage states that the book popularized the discovery, which matches the statement that it became widely known because of Gould's book.

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:

Why: The statement claims it includes impressions of soft and hard body parts, which directly matches the passage's mention of soft body parts alongside bones and shells.

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Although the fossil bed was discovered on a mountain, these animals originally existed below an ocean, the bed of which was later pushed up to create the Rockies."
Why: The passage explicitly states that the animals originally lived below an ocean, contradicting the statement that they were land animals.

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8

Why: The passage states that Hallucigenia is an ancestor of modern arthropods, which directly contradicts the claim that it is unrelated to any modern creature.

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4

Why: The note asks for the period following which the Burgess Shale was formed, and the text explicitly states it began to form soon after the "Cambrian explosion".

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "American paleontologist Charles Walcott, following reports of fabulous fossil finds by construction workers on a Canadian railway who were digging in the mountains in the late 19th century, is said to have tripped over a block of shale in 1909 that revealed the area's remarkable supply of specimens."
Why: The note states that Walcott learned of the finds from people building something, and the passage specifies these were construction workers building a "railway".

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Weirdest of all was Hallucigenia, described by paleontologist Simon Conway Morris, when he re-examined Walcott's specimens in 1979."
Why: The note refers to a researcher looking at Burgess Shale findings again, matching the text where Simon Conway Morris "re-examined" the specimens in the year "1979".

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "This suggests that the evolution of such complex life went on uninterrupted."
Why: The note states that discoveries in Morocco show that the process of complex life forms continuing was uninterrupted, and the passage confirms this was the "evolution" of such life.

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:

Why: The table asks for the shape of Opabinia's tail, and the text explicitly states it had "a tail in the shape of a fan".

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:

Why: The table asks what Nectocaris looked like, and the text says it "could be mistaken for a leech".

title: The Burgess Shale Fossils
explanation:

title: The development of plastics

title: The development of plastics
explanation:

title: The development of plastics

explanation:

title: The Economic Effect of Climate

title: The Economic Effect of Climate
explanation:

title: The Economic Effect of Climate

explanation:

title: The English canal system

title: The English canal system
explanation:

Why: The statement says they were funded differently, which directly agrees with the passage stating English canals were paid for by merchants while European canals were financed by the aristocracy.

title: The English canal system
explanation:

title: The English canal system
explanation:

title: The English canal system

title: The English canal system
explanation:

title: The English canal system
explanation:

title: The English canal system
explanation:

title: The English canal system
explanation:

title: The English canal system
explanation:

title: The English canal system

title: The English canal system

title: The history of the guitar

title: The history of the guitar

title: The history of the guitar
explanation:

title: The history of the guitar

title: The history of the guitar
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "The earliest guitar-like instruments to arrive in Europe had, most often, four strings. Many such instruments, and variations with from three to five strings, can be seen in mediaeval illustrated manuscripts."
Why: The passage states that these instruments had variations ranging from "three to five strings", which directly contradicts the claim that they all had the same number of strings.

title: The history of the guitar
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "When the four-stringed Persian chartar arrived in Spain, however, it changed in form and construction, acquiring pairs of strings tuned to the same note instead of single strings."
Why: The table states the chitarra developed from an earlier instrument, which Paragraph 7 identifies as the Persian "chartar" when it arrived in Spain.

title: The history of the guitar
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "The modern classical guitar first appeared in its current form in the mid-19th century, when the Spanish guitar maker Antonio Torres increased the size of the body, altered its proportions, and introduced the revolutionary fan-braced top."
Why: The table asks for a modification made by Antonio Torres to shape the classical guitar, and the text specifies that he increased the size of the "body".

title: The history of the guitar
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "His design radically increased the volume and improved the tone of the instrument, and very soon became the norm."
Why: The table mentions that Torres's changes produced a better tone and greater "volume", which directly matches the text stating his design radically increased the volume.

title: The history of the guitar
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "At the time when Torres made his breakthrough, German immigrants to America – among them Christian Fredrich Martin – began making guitars with X-braced tops."
Why: The table asks where X-braced top guitars were first made in the mid-19th century, and the text notes that German immigrants began making them in "America".

title: The history of the guitar
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "Steel strings, which became widely available several decades later in the early 1900s, offered the promise of a much louder guitar, but the increased tension was too much for the fan-braced top."
Why: The table refers to strings that became available around 1900, which the passage identifies as "steel" strings.

title: The history of the guitar
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "The electric guitar was born when pickups were fitted to Hawaiian and jazz guitars in the late 1920s, but met with little success until 1936, when Gibson introduced its famous ES150 model."
Why: The table asks what was added to guitars in the 1920s to create the electric guitar, and the text states that "pickups" were fitted to them.

title: The history of the guitar
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "The electric guitar was born when pickups were fitted to Hawaiian and jazz guitars in the late 1920s, but met with little success until 1936, when Gibson introduced its famous ES150 model."
Why: The table refers to a well-known version of the electric guitar brought out in 1936, which was introduced by "Gibson".

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "These first two failed to capture the imagination and the dollars of industrialists or of the public, but the third image of the home of the future did."
Why: This sentence shows that the three early visions of the future home had mixed results—two failed while the third succeeded—making "Mixed success for visions of the future" the correct summary.

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Appliance manufacturers, advertisers and women's magazines teamed up to surround women with images of the technology of tomorrow that would 'automate' their lives, and automation became a synonym for reduced domestic labor."
Why: The paragraph describes how new kitchen technology aimed to automate and lighten domestic chores, which directly explains why "Housework declines in the house of the future" fits the section.

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "A 1968 Whirlpool ad in Ladies’ Home Journal (“How Whirlpool made my husband a man again”) framed a crisis of masculinity triggered by men doing housework, “solved” by the two-speed dishwasher—essentially preserving traditional roles."
Why: The section discusses social tensions around who did household chores and how appliances supposedly resolved conflicts between men and women, matching "The house of the future helps with the battle of the sexes."

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "The 1970s looked backward to pioneer heritage."
Why: The paragraph explains a shift in architectural and lifestyle priorities during the 1970s away from high-tech towards traditional materials like wood, blurred indoor and outdoor boundaries, and a focus on nature, representing "A change of structure in the home of tomorrow."

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "In the 1980s, as more women worked outside the home and household computing emerged, enthusiasm for technology rebounded."
Why: FLAG: The provided heading 'The future lies in the past' and correct answer VII do not match the content of Paragraph E, which actually discusses 1970s nostalgia in Paragraph D.

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Trust in science and technology eroded; utopian techno-futures waned."
Why: A loss of faith in automation is directly paraphrased by the erosion of trust in science and technology and the decline of utopian techno-futures.

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "The second conception was that of the mass-produced, prefabricated house, a dwelling potentially available to every North American."
Why: A house made in a factory matches the idea of a "mass-produced, prefabricated house" mentioned in the text.

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "In the 1980s, as more women worked outside the home and household computing emerged, enthusiasm for technology rebounded."
Why: The text states that "more women worked outside the home," meaning there were fewer full-time housewives staying at home during the day.

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "solar tech and the Green movement rose amid energy-crisis concerns."
Why: An increased awareness of the environment is reflected in the rise of the "Green movement" and "solar tech."

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Appliance manufacturers, advertisers and women's magazines teamed up to surround women with images of the technology of tomorrow that would 'automate' their lives, and automation became a synonym for reduced domestic labor."
Why: The connection between the future of technology and consumerism (driven by advertisers and appliance manufacturers targeting women) is shown here.

title: The house of the future, then and now
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "The term 'home of tomorrow' first came into usage in the 1920s to describe the 'ideal house for future living (Corn and Horrigan, 1984, p. 62)."
Why: The introduction of a new phrase ("home of tomorrow") to describe the perfect home ("ideal house for future living") is explicitly stated here.

title: The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "The law influences all of us virtually all the time."
Why: This opening sentence introduces the main idea of the paragraph, which is how the law governs almost all aspects of our daily existence and experiences throughout our lives.

title: The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Today, by contrast, a vast number of people can read, and it is becoming easier for people to take an interest in law, and for the general population to help actually shape the law in many countries."
Why: This sentence captures the core theme of the paragraph, explaining how increased literacy allows ordinary people to engage with and actively influence the legal system.

title: The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "In our rapidly developing world, all sorts of skills and knowledge are valuable."
Why: This topic sentence sets up a comparison between different forms of professional expertise—such as IT skills and legal understanding—and explains why legal knowledge is universally vital.

title: The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "The number of laws has never been greater."
Why: This direct statement introduces the main theme of the paragraph, which is supported by statistics showing the massive growth in the volume of laws and Acts produced over time.

title: The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "However, despite their important role in developing the rules, lawyers are not universally admired."
Why: This sentence encapsulates the central idea of the paragraph, which explores the long-standing negative public perception and jokes directed at lawyers.

title: The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "But, in general, it is no more just to say that lawyers are bad because they make a living from people’s problems than it is to make the same accusation in respect of nurses or IT consultants."
Why: This sentence highlights the core argument of the paragraph, providing justifications for why general criticisms of lawyers are unjustified and based on misunderstandings of their work.

title: The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "But legal understanding is just as vital and as universally needed."
Why: This statement matches the idea that knowing the law is just as important as having IT and computer skills, which are discussed in the same paragraph.

title: The Importance of Law
explanation:
Where: Paragraph C
Quote: "In other words, the lawyer is the only person who has read and made sense of the rules."
Why: This supports the conclusion that society relies on legal experts to make sense of the rules because without them, people would not be able to navigate problems successfully.

title: The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "In 1882, domestic electricity at last became a possibility when Thomas Edison's company started providing electricity on a commercial basis."
Why: The table asks for the year when electricity was first supplied to homeowners, which corresponds to "1882" in the text.

title: The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "As electricity became more widely available, electrical products began to come onto the market, starting with the electric sewing machine in 1889."
Why: The table lists the sewing machine as the first appliance (1889) and asks for the last one mentioned in the 1889-1918 period, which is the electric dishwasher (1918).

title: The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "By 1930, 70 per cent of US households, some 20 million homes, were electrified — up from ten per cent in 1910 — and more than the rest of the world combined at that point in time."
Why: The table asks for the year when 10% of US households had electricity, which the text gives as "1910".

title: The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "In that year, people spent $175 million on them."
Why: The text links the $175 million spending figure directly to the year "1917", which fits the table row requirement.

title: The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Much the same happened with a small company called Frigidaire, founded in 1918, which saw an opening for a refrigerator designed for the home and so successfully seized the opportunity that the name almost became generic, although it took until 1927 for General Electric to produce the first million-selling model."
Why: The table refers to General Electric's million-selling model produced in 1927, which was a domestic "refrigerator".

title: The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "The proportion would have been higher still except that rural electrification took so long to complete; even by 1946, as little as half of US farms had electricity."
Why: The table states that only 50% of a certain group had electricity by the end of 1946, and the text identifies this group as "farms".

title: The introduction of gas and electricity to the US
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "by the end of that decade, with almost every household owning at least one, market saturation was practically complete."
Why: The table notes that in 1930 there was a "radio" in nearly every home, which matches the conclusion of the previous sentence about the radio being the most successful product and achieving complete market saturation by the end of the decade.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "In a recent study, researchers traveled all over the world to examine sleep in some of the world's last remaining hunter-gatherer societies - the Hadza of Tanzania, the San of Namibia, and the Tsimane of Bolivia."
Why: This sentence captures the study of preindustrial societies used to uncover ancient sleep patterns, matching the heading about analyzing old or traditional sources to discover sleep habits.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "Instead of going to sleep right at dusk, tribespeople were staying awake an average of between 2.5 and 4.4 hours after sunset."
Why: It details the scientific findings about the natural sleeping and waking cycles of these groups, corresponding to the heading about natural phenomena related to sleep.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "They found that it also played a big role, though was somewhat less important than light in influencing sleep patterns."
Why: This section explores how environmental elements like light and temperature dictate when sleep occurs, matching the heading about environmental factors affecting sleep.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "Importantly, almost none of them were troubled by sleeplessness."
Why: It highlights the contrast between modern sleeplessness and the rare occurrence of sleep difficulties in traditional societies, aligning with the heading about factors preventing sleep.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "If we can't blame our health problems on our lack of sleep, could it be that the reason we feel so unrested is because of poor health?"
Why: This concluding part questions the link between lack of sleep and common illnesses, matching the heading about potential health issues related to sleep.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "Instead of going to sleep right at dusk, tribespeople were staying awake an average of between 2.5 and 4.4 hours after sunset."
Why: The summary states that people habitually went to bed early, soon after a specific time of day related to the setting sun, which the passage identifies as "dusk".

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "Indications from both science and history suggest that the eight-hour sleep may not be a natural or inborn pattern for humans."
Why: This heading matches because the section discusses scientific research, specifically Thomas Wehr's experiment, proving that divided sleep is our natural biological rhythm.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "In 2001, historian Roger Ekirch of Virginia Tech University in the US published a paper drawn from 16 years of research, revealing historical evidence that humans used to sleep in two distinct periods of time each night."
Why: This heading fits as the text details how the historian analyzed historical records and documents from various eras to uncover the past existence of a segmented sleeping pattern.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph D
Quote: "This could be the cause of a condition called sleep maintenance insomnia, where people wake during the night and have trouble getting back to sleep."
Why: The heading is accurate because it focuses on how a modern medical condition (insomnia) can arise from a mismatch between our natural preference for divided sleep and modern habits.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Sleep psychologist, Gregg Jacobs, says that the idea that we must sleep for an extended period of time could be damaging if it makes people who wake up in the night anxious, as this anxiety can itself discourage sleep and is likely to affect waking life too."
Why: This matches the heading because experts explain how psychological factors (anxiety about waking up) and environmental expectations prevent people from returning to sleep, leading to further problems.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "'Associations with night before the 17th century were not good,' he writes."
Why: Craig Koslofsky explains that danger from thieves at night made people scared of the streets, which caused them to stay indoors and maintain a divided sleep pattern.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "They sometimes got up and moved around the house, although most people stayed in bed, and perhaps read or wrote if they had enough money for candles."
Why: Roger Ekirch's historical research shows that during the night waking periods, people engaged in various activities like moving around, reading, writing, or analyzing dreams.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "Sleep psychologist, Gregg Jacobs, says that the idea that we must sleep for an extended period of time could be damaging if it makes people who wake up in the night anxious, as this anxiety can itself discourage sleep and is likely to affect waking life too."
Why: Gregg Jacobs states that believing we must sleep continuously can cause harmful anxiety in people who wake up during the night.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "Much like Wehr's findings, these references describe a first sleep which began not long following sunset."
Why: The text states that the first sleep began "not long following sunset," which matches the summary's mention that people went to bed early, soon after sunset.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "In many historic accounts, Ekirch found that people used the time that they were awake between periods of sleep to think about and attempt to analyse their dreams."
Why: The text mentions that people used their waking time to "analyse their dreams," directly matching the summary's reference to considering the meaning of their dreams.

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:
Where: Paragraph B
Quote: "He goes on to explain that the streets of the cities and towns at night were often populated by thieves or worse."
Why: The text explains that people stayed at home because the streets were populated by "thieves," which fits the summary's statement that they feared thieves on unlit streets.

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "The concept of the national park originated in America, though it was quickly replicated by similar parks in Canada, Finland, New Zealand, Australia, and elsewhere."
Why: The statement says America copied the idea from other countries, but the passage contradicts this by stating that the concept originated in America.

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "Yellowstone comprises some 3,500 square miles of wilderness and today attracts more than four million visitors a year."
Why: The passage mentions how many visitors Yellowstone gets, but it does not compare its visitor numbers to other parks to say it is the *most* frequently visited.

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "They are administered by the National Parks Service (NPS), which also manages significant monuments and historic structures such as the Statue of Liberty, the Gettysburg Museum, and Ford’s Theatre, where President Lincoln was assassinated."
Why: The statement matches the passage's explanation that the NPS manages both natural parks and historic buildings/monuments.

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "In 1832, the painter George Catlin dreamed of creating ‘a nation’s park’ to preserve the grasslands in the state of South Dakota."
Why: The passage mentions Catlin's proposal for a park and notes that he failed to see it established, but it provides no information about anyone criticising him for it.

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "Four years later, the writer Ralph Waldo Emerson published an important essay entitled Nature, in which he argued that natural landscapes should be protected rather than exploited for agriculture and commerce."
Why: The statement says Emerson believed land should be used freely for farms and businesses, but the passage contradicts this by stating he argued landscapes should be *protected* rather than exploited for those things.

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The creation of a public park in the Yosemite Valley was directly the result of his work."
Why: The statement matches the passage, which confirms that a park in Yosemite Valley was created as a direct result of Olmsted's work.

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "The Yellowstone National Park not only preserved the headwaters of the Mississippi, Colorado, and Snake rivers, but also provided a sanctuary for countless endangered species by imposing a ban on hunting in all its forms."
Why: The note asks what type of activity was prohibited (banned) in Yellowstone, and the text explicitly states that there was "a ban on hunting in all its forms."

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "In recognition of the difficulties of running these vast wilderness areas, their management was for many years placed in the hands of the military, rather than the federal or state government."
Why: The note asks who administered the parks, and the passage explains that their management was given to the "military."

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Increasingly, these ran through even the most remote areas, where many parks were located, making tourism possible in these locations for the very first time."
Why: The note states that the railroad system encouraged new kinds of activity, and the text links the railways directly to making "tourism possible."

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Nathaniel Langford was instrumental in setting up Yellowstone and saw the park as an ideal opportunity for the education of ordinary citizens in all aspects of the natural world and environmental conservation, which was his number one priority."
Why: The note asks what Langford believed was the most important role (his "number one priority"), and the text identifies this as the "education" of ordinary citizens.

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "However, arguably even more important was Mather’s transformation of the hitherto poorly managed finances of the parks."
Why: The note mentions that Mather greatly improved something relating to the parks, and the text confirms he transformed their "finances."

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "However, the controversial decision to permit the construction of dams in national parks was made on the basis that the resulting supplies of water and hydroelectric power would be in the public interest."
Why: The note states that the NPS allowed certain structures to be built, and the text specifies that they permitted the construction of "dams."

title: The National Parks of America
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "Then in the 1930s, the number of visitors expanded dramatically, largely because mass-produced automobiles became affordable, allowing ever more city-dwellers to reach the park network."
Why: The note refers to the 1930s and what became available to increase park popularity, and the text points to the availability of "automobiles."

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "The light material of silk was sometimes used, but was normally too expensive to consider."
Why: The passage states that silk was "sometimes used," which directly matches the statement that writing was "occasionally" done on it.

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "During the same period, according to a written account, tea was served from baskets with multi-colored paper cups and paper napkins of different sizes and shapes."
Why: The passage mentions that multi-colored paper cups were used during the Tang Dynasty, but it does not state that *colored paper was invented* then; invention and usage are different facts, making this NOT GIVEN.

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "During a battle on the banks of the Tarus river, a Chinese caravan was captured which happened to include several papermakers."
Why: The statement claims that papermakers from Samarkand were captured by the Chinese, whereas the passage states the opposite: a Chinese caravan including papermakers was captured.

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "The rudimentary and laborious process of papermaking was refined and bulk manufacturing of paper began in Iran, where they invented a method to make a thicker sheet of paper, which helped transform papermaking from an art into an important business."
Why: "Bulk manufacturing" in the passage means large-scale industry, and it states this began in Iran, matching the question.

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8
Quote: "Finally, when the Moors from North Africa invaded Spain and Portugal they brought the technology with them and so it was that papermaking entered Europe in the 12th century."
Why: The passage confirms that the Moors brought papermaking technology from North Africa into Europe (Spain and Portugal).

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 9
Quote: "The notion of paper being used as a practical everyday item did not occur until the 15th century when Johannes Gutenberg perfected movable type printing, which included the use of metal molds and alloys, a special press, and oil-based inks, allowing the mass production of printed books."
Why: While the passage discusses Gutenberg and the use of paper, it never mentions whether paper materials were very expensive at that time.

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 10
Quote: "Yet soon this source became insufficient and some curious attempts were made to find new materials."
Why: The passage states the rag trade ended because the source of rags became "insufficient," not because of transport difficulties as the statement claims.

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 1
Quote: "The Egyptians cut the plant into strips which they softened in water."
Why: The table row for Egypt mentions that a plant's parts were softened, woven, and pounded; the passage specifies that the Egyptians cut the plant into "strips".

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "In fact, it has been estimated that a single book written on parchment required the skins of 300 sheep."
Why: The Europe row refers to parchment made from animal skins such as this animal, which the text identifies as "sheep".

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The skins had to be specifically prepared by drying them and they were then stretched on a special frame."
Why: The Europe row describes the production method for parchment as being dried and then having undergone this action, which the text gives as "stretched".

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "They were taken away to Samarkand, which was a good place to make paper because it had an abundant supply of hemp and flax."
Why: The table row for the date 751 AD requires the place where flax and hemp were used, which the passage identifies as "Samarkand".

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "They began to prepare it in stone mills and Samarkand became an important papermaking
center."
Why: The row for 751 AD states that mills made of this material were used, and the text specifies "stone" mills.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 2
Quote: "The earliest occupation of Patagonia carries obvious implications for understanding when the North and South American continents were peopled, because it gives a baseline that all calculations regarding the rate of dispersion of humans throughout both continents must take into account."
Why: The question asks about the writer's main point regarding migration to Patagonia. Option B restates this as having an impact on research into the wider region by providing a baseline for calculations about human dispersion across both North and South America.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Some scholars accepted a human presence in the Americas as early as 20,000 years ago, while others proposed that it could date no earlier than 8,000 years ago, and the debate is still with us today."
Why: The question asks for the writer's purpose in the second paragraph. Option D correctly identifies this purpose as summarising a scholarly debate, which the text demonstrates by outlining opposing views on the timeframe of the settlement of the Americas.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "Herein lies a second debate which revolves around the question of how migration is to be understood."
Why: The question asks why the writer refers to the "Late model". Option A explains that it is discussed in comparison with another theory of migration, namely the "early" model that many scholars now support.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 4
Quote: "This has always been difficult to take seriously and many scholars now support the idea of an ‘early’ model that sees the migration as a less ordered migration, and this is surely the most realistic scenario as migrants slowly adapted to the diverse natural habitats they would have met while travelling through the continent."
Why: The question asks for the main point about the 'early' model. Option A restates the idea that it is the most realistic scenario because migrants slowly adapted to the diverse natural habitats they encountered, making it consistent with the physical conditions of the land.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 5
Quote: "Nevertheless, evidence for human occupation of the centre of South America is now securely dated to around 12,500 years ago at the Monte Verde site, which casts doubt on the ‘late model’."
Why: The question asks what is suggested about the Monte Verde site. Option C restates the idea that the site provides supporting evidence for a relatively early settlement because it is securely dated to 12,500 years ago, thereby casting doubt on the late model.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "We can speculate then that the retreat of the Patagonian glaciers around 14,000 years ago allowed the initial human intrusion into a pristine environment, which was similar to that of early post-glacial Europe."
Why: The question claims the conditions were unique, but the writer states they were actually similar to those of early post-glacial Europe.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "Human settlement of the vast horizontal expanse of treeless high country must have been tenuous at best, and the evidence for this occupation remains relatively scant, most of it coming from rock shelters in Argentina and Chile."
Why: The passage mentions human settlement in the high country and evidence from rock shelters, but the writer never states whether or not the migrants hunted wild animals for food.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "There is, however, reliable evidence from these sites to confirm the presence of humans by around 11,000 years ago in different habitats, and some hints of an even older occupation."
Why: The question claims archaeologists failed to draw conclusions from rock shelters, but the writer states there is reliable evidence confirming human presence from these sites.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 6
Quote: "This is because anthropologists have come to recognise that bones or other evidence may be deposited in caves by natural agency, in other words by other forces such as floods or predators, and not necessarily by humans."
Why: The writer agrees that archaeological evidence like bones can be moved from place to place by natural forces such as floods or predators.

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "They were buried in layers of peat, which has the property of preserving wood remarkably well, and as a result radiocarbon dating tests have shown these artefacts to date from around 12,500 years ago."
Why: The passage states that the peat preserved the wood "remarkably well," which is paraphrased in the summary by the choice "good condition".

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "However, the evidence from this site has recently been called into question, because dispersed flecks of carbon used in the test process were taken unsystematically from many different places in the site."
Why: The passage mentions samples being taken "unsystematically," which corresponds to the summary choice "random collection".

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 7
Quote: "About 150 kilometres south is the site called El Ceibo, where a similar collection of artefacts to that found at Los Toldos has been discovered from the lowest levels of the dig, but as yet no radiocarbon dates are available and this sort of analysis of the existing evidence is required before the site’s value can be confirmed."
Why: The passage states that analysis (such as radiocarbon dating) is required to confirm the site's value, which is paraphrased as "scientific evaluation".

title: The People of Patagonia
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 8

explanation:

title: The Pirah people of Brazil
explanation:

explanation:

title: The Pirah people of Brazil
explanation:

title: The Pirah people of Brazil

title: The Pirah people of Brazil
explanation:

title: The Pirah people of Brazil
explanation:

title: The Pirah people of Brazil
explanation:

title: The Pirah people of Brazil

title: The Pirah people of Brazil
explanation:

title: The Pirah people of Brazil

title: The Pirah people of Brazil
explanation:

title: The Pirah people of Brazil

explanation:

Why: The text states that these skinks do not "hibernate" or lie "dormant for extended periods," which is paraphrased in the summary as not requiring a long "winter sleep."

title: The Myth of the Eight-hour Sleep
explanation:

title: The Origin of Paper
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Ts'ai Lun seems to have made his paper by mixing finely chopped mulberry bark and hemp rags with water, mashing the mixture flat with a stone mortar, and then pressing out the water and letting it dry in the sun."
Why: The table asks for the materials used in China in 105 AD, specifically mentioning "hemp rags" and the bark of a mulberry tree; the passage refers to this as "mulberry bark".

title: The power of music
explanation:

Why: The question asks about people who were previously helped by this type of music, which corresponds to the "disabled patients" mentioned in the text.

title: The Purpose of Facial Expressions
explanation:
Where: Paragraph A
Quote: "In fact, since the 1970s Ekman has dominated the field of emotion research with his theory that when an emotion occurs, a large number of electrical impulses also occur, creating specific facial expressions and other physiological changes, such as increased or decreased heart rate or heightened blood pressure."
Why: The phrase "physiological changes, such as increased or decreased heart rate or heightened blood pressure" directly corresponds to "changes inside the body when an emotion is felt."

title: The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph E
Quote: "This research adds to a growing body of literature suggesting that sleep can reorganise information to facilitate problem-solving,” says Kristin Sanders, first author of the study and a doctoral student at Northwestern University."
Why: The statement claims that information related to a problem can be restructured during sleep, which directly mirrors Kristin Sanders' quote that sleep can "reorganise information to facilitate problem-solving."

title: The Science of “Sleeping on It”
explanation:
Where: Paragraph F
Quote: "According to Barrett, all functions of the brain must have some practical purpose rooted in evolution and natural selection, which may explain why the brain uses dreams to break down, analyse, and solve problems."
Why: The statement says all brain functions must have evolved for a particular purpose, which is a direct paraphrase of Deirdre Barrett's view that "all functions of the brain must have some practical purpose rooted in evolution and natural selection."

title: Verbal and non-Verbal messages
explanation:

title: What is social history?
explanation:
Where: Paragraph 3
Quote: "Whereas traditional history had focused on the 12th to 17th centuries, social history was apt to make its historical homeland in the 19th century, while latterly, it has even begun to extend its inquiry up to contemporary events and movements."
Why: The writer explicitly confirms that traditional history concentrated on the 12th to 17th centuries, whereas social history focused on the later 19th century, directly agreeing with the statement.
